intro: Eighteen states are running a **back-to-school sales tax holiday in 2026** — a window of a weekend to a full month when clothing, school supplies, and in some states computers are exempt from state sales tax. The dates and rules differ wildly: **Texas, Ohio, Missouri, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Virginia** share the **August 7-9** weekend, **Florida** runs a month-long window (**July 20 - August 20**), **Illinois** only cuts its rate from 6.25% to 1.25% instead of a full exemption, and **Connecticut** closes the season **August 16-22**. Every state also sets **per-item price caps** — and they're all-or-nothing: a $110 pair of sneakers in Texas (cap: under $100) is fully taxable, not taxable on the excess. Pick your state below, enter what you plan to spend on clothing, school supplies, and a computer, and this calculator tells you the **exact dates for your state**, whether each item **qualifies under the cap**, and **how many dollars of tax you skip**. For a plain add-or-reverse tax computation any day of the year, use the [Sales Tax Calculator](/en/sales-tax-calculator), and to plan the whole shopping list first, try the [Back-to-School Budget Calculator](/en/back-to-school-budget-calculator).
keyTakeaway: A $500 back-to-school cart in Texas (Aug 7-9, 6.25% waived) saves about $31 in tax — but only if every clothing or supply item is under the $100 per-item cap; one $120 jacket stays fully taxable.

explanation:
## What is a sales tax holiday?

A sales tax holiday is a legislated window when a state suspends its sales tax on specific categories — typically clothing, school supplies, and sometimes computers — to ease back-to-school costs. In 2026, **18 states** run one. The savings equal the **state tax rate waived times your qualifying cart**: a $500 qualifying cart in Tennessee (7%, state and local waived) skips about $35 of tax; the same cart in Missouri (4.225% state rate) skips about $21.

## 2026 Dates and Rules by State

| State | 2026 Dates | Clothing cap | Supplies cap | Computers cap | State rate waived |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mississippi | Jul 10-12 | under $100 | under $100 | not covered | 7% |
| Alabama | Jul 17-19 | $156 | $78 | $1,173 | 4% |
| Florida | Jul 20 - Aug 20 | $100 | $50 | $1,500 | 6% |
| Tennessee | Jul 31 - Aug 2 | $100 | $100 | $1,500 | 7% |
| New Mexico | Jul 31 - Aug 2 | under $100 | under $30 | $1,000 | 4.875% |
| West Virginia | Jul 31 - Aug 3 | $125 | $50 | $500 (laptops/tablets) | 6% |
| Arkansas | Aug 1-2 | under $100 | no cap | no cap (electronics) | 6.5% |
| Iowa | Aug 7-8 | under $100 | not covered | not covered | 6% |
| Texas | Aug 7-9 | under $100 | under $100 | not covered | 6.25% |
| Ohio | Aug 7-9 | $75 | $20 | not covered | 5.75% |
| Missouri | Aug 7-9 | $100 | $50 | $1,500 | 4.225% |
| Oklahoma | Aug 7-9 | under $100 | not covered | not covered | 4.5% |
| South Carolina | Aug 7-9 | no cap | no cap | no cap | 6% |
| Virginia | Aug 7-9 | $100 | $20 | not covered | 5.3% |
| Illinois | Aug 7-16 | under $125 | no cap | not covered | 5 pts (6.25% → 1.25%) |
| Massachusetts | Aug 8-9 | $2,500 (any item) | $2,500 | $2,500 | 6.25% |
| Maryland | Aug 9-15 | $100 | not covered* | not covered | 6% |
| Connecticut | Aug 16-22 | under $300 | not covered | not covered | 6.35% |

*Maryland exempts the first $40 of a backpack. Louisiana no longer holds a back-to-school holiday — it was repealed. Sources: state Departments of Revenue via Tax Foundation, *Sales Tax Holidays by State, 2026*.

## The cap is all-or-nothing

This is the #1 misunderstanding. Price caps apply **per item**, and an item over the cap is **fully taxable**, not taxable only on the excess. A $110 pair of sneakers in Texas (cap: under $100) pays 8.25% combined tax on all $110 — about $9.08 — while a $99 pair pays $0. If you're near a cap, splitting purchases (two $60 hoodies instead of one $120 jacket) is completely legal and saves real money.

## State vs. local tax

Most holidays waive the **state** portion of the tax. Whether county and city add-ons are also waived varies: Texas, Tennessee, Missouri, and Arkansas waive local tax too, while in some Alabama and other jurisdictions localities opt in individually. This calculator uses the state-level rate waived as the baseline, so in states that also waive local tax your real savings are **higher** than shown — in Texas the full combined rate is up to 8.25%.

## Formula

```
For each category (clothing, supplies, computer):
  if category not covered in state       → savings = 0
  if priciest item > per-item cap        → that item excluded (fully taxable)
  qualifying_amount × (rate_waived/100)  → category savings

total_savings = clothing + supplies + computer savings
```

## Worked Example — Texas, Aug 7-9

| Item | Amount | Qualifies? | Tax skipped (6.25%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clothing cart | $250 (priciest item $80) | Yes, under $100/item | $15.63 |
| School supplies | $120 (priciest $45) | Yes | $7.50 |
| Laptop $600 | — | No — TX doesn't cover computers | $0 |
| **Total** | **$970 cart** | | **$23.13** |

In Texas the local tax is also waived, so at the 8.25% combined Houston rate the real savings on the qualifying $370 are about $30.53.

## Strategy tips

- **Computers**: only Florida, Tennessee, Missouri ($1,500), Alabama ($1,173), New Mexico ($1,000), West Virginia ($500), Arkansas and South Carolina (no cap) exempt them. If you live in Texas or Ohio, the holiday does nothing for a laptop.
- **Online orders count** in every holiday state if ordered and paid within the window — delivery can arrive later.
- **Massachusetts is the wildcard**: its Aug 8-9 holiday covers almost *any* retail item up to $2,500, not just school gear.
- **Illinois is the trap**: shoppers expect 0% and still pay 1.25% state + full local tax. Savings are real but smaller.
- Stack the holiday with retailer back-to-school promos — the tax exemption applies to the **discounted** price, which can pull an over-cap item under the cap.

Budget the whole list first with the [Back-to-School Budget Calculator](/en/back-to-school-budget-calculator), and for everyday rates in the other 32 states use the [Sales Tax Calculator](/en/sales-tax-calculator). If the shopping season strains the family budget, the [50/30/20 Family Budget Calculator](/en/50-30-20-family-budget) helps rebalance the month.

> **Note:** Always confirm final rules with your state's Department of Revenue before a big purchase — states occasionally adjust item lists close to the date.

faq.q: Which states have a back-to-school sales tax holiday in 2026?
faq.a: Eighteen states: Mississippi (Jul 10-12), Alabama (Jul 17-19), Florida (Jul 20-Aug 20), Tennessee and New Mexico (Jul 31-Aug 2), West Virginia (Jul 31-Aug 3), Arkansas (Aug 1-2), Iowa (Aug 7-8), Texas, Ohio, Missouri, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Virginia (Aug 7-9), Illinois (Aug 7-16, rate cut to 1.25%), Massachusetts (Aug 8-9), Maryland (Aug 9-15), and Connecticut (Aug 16-22). Louisiana repealed its holiday, and big states like California, New York (statewide), Georgia, and Pennsylvania don't hold one.

faq.q: When is the Texas tax-free weekend in 2026?
faq.a: August 7-9, 2026 (Friday through Sunday). Clothing, footwear, school supplies, and backpacks priced under $100 per item are exempt from both state (6.25%) and local sales tax. Computers are NOT included in the Texas holiday.

faq.q: Are laptops and computers included in the 2026 tax-free weekends?
faq.a: Only in some states: Florida ($1,500 or less), Tennessee ($1,500), Missouri ($1,500), Alabama ($1,173 for computers/software), New Mexico ($1,000), West Virginia ($500 for laptops/tablets), and Arkansas and South Carolina with no price cap. Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Oklahoma, Virginia, Maryland, and Connecticut do not exempt computers.

faq.q: If my item costs more than the cap, do I pay tax only on the excess?
faq.a: No — caps are all-or-nothing in every state. A $110 shirt in a state with a $100 cap is fully taxable on the entire $110. There's no partial exemption, so buying two cheaper items instead of one expensive one can legitimately save you the full tax.

faq.q: Do online purchases qualify for the sales tax holiday?
faq.a: Yes. In all 2026 holiday states, an online order qualifies if it is ordered and paid for during the holiday window, even if delivery happens afterward. The item still has to meet the category and per-item price cap rules of the destination state.

faq.q: Is the Florida back-to-school holiday really a whole month?
faq.a: Yes. Florida's 2026 back-to-school window runs July 20 through August 20 — clothing and footwear $100 or less, school supplies $50 or less, learning aids $30 or less, and personal computers $1,500 or less are exempt from the 6% state tax for the entire month.

faq.q: Why does Illinois save me less than other states?
faq.a: Illinois doesn't fully exempt purchases. During August 7-16, 2026 the state portion of the rate drops from 6.25% to 1.25% on qualifying clothing (under $125/item) and school supplies — a 5-point savings — but you still pay the remaining 1.25% state rate plus all local taxes.

faq.q: Does the holiday waive local (city/county) sales tax too?
faq.a: It depends on the state. Texas, Tennessee, Missouri, and Arkansas waive local tax along with the state tax, so your savings equal the full combined rate. In others, localities decide individually (parts of Alabama) or local tax always still applies (Illinois). This calculator uses the state-level rate as a conservative baseline.

faq.q: Does Louisiana have a sales tax holiday in 2026?
faq.a: No. Louisiana repealed its annual sales tax holidays; there is no 2026 back-to-school tax-free window there. If a listing mentions Louisiana dates in August, it's outdated — check the Louisiana Department of Revenue.

faq.q: Do discounts and coupons count toward the price cap?
faq.a: Yes, in most states the cap is tested against the final price actually paid after retailer discounts. A $120 backpack marked down to $95 qualifies under a $100 cap. Manufacturer coupons reimbursed to the retailer can be treated differently in some states — check your state's DOR guidance for edge cases.
